deep.reconstruction:
There is no derivation, formula or computation on this page. Folio 1r of Math. 33 holds about seven ink and pencil drawings of knots and bends in practical cordage, with brief captions. Reading the image from top to bottom:

(a) Top left (ink). One cord passes as a bight or loop around a horizontal cord, with its two ends led upward. It is a simple hitch or binding knot, roughly a lark's head or cow hitch type.

(b) Top right (ink), captioned 'Weber Kn.' (Weberknoten, i.e. weaver's knot). Two cords are joined by a small interlaced knot with ends trailing to both sides. This is the weaver's knot, which is topologically the sheet bend.

(c) Upper left (pencil). A long loop (eye) closed by a knot near its top, with a free end leaving to the right. It resembles a bowline or a loop made with a sheet-bend-type nip.

(d) Upper middle (ink). Two parallel horizontal pairs of strands enter from left and right and interlace in a large symmetric oval with crossings at the waist. It is a loosely drawn bend joining two ropes, of the reef or carrick type.

(e) Right middle (ink, with a pencil sketch beside it). An interlaced oval knot with one end leaving diagonally upward and others leaving left and right. A faint pencil caption below reads 'Weber Kn.', so it is presumably another view or variant of the weaver's knot / sheet bend. Small double strokes mark crossings.

(f) Lower middle (ink). Two strands with diagonal ends interlace through two overlapping lobes. Its shape and its alternating over/under pattern are those of the classic carrick bend (Josephine knot).

(g) Bottom, large (ink over pencil). A decorative knot with four elongated bights or ends (up, left, right, down) radiating from a central interwoven core of overlapping rings, giving a pinwheel or cross shape. It is an ornamental four-lobed knot of the kind found in sailors' or ornamental knot books.

At the foot of the page, in Gauss's hand, is a bibliographic note: 'Riedl, Beiträge zur Theorie der Sehnenwinkel[?]. Wien. 1827'. The last word is hard to read. Top left is the archival shelfmark 'Gauß, Math 33'; top right is the old number 487/1, struck through, and the folio number (1).

Purpose (my inference): the page records concrete knot types, mostly bends joining two cords (weaver's knot / sheet bend, carrick bend), as material for Gauss's interest in a 'geometria situs' of entangled curves. That interest is documented elsewhere in his enumeration of plane closed curves by crossing sequences ('Tractfiguren') and in the 1833 linking-number integral. The dated reference (1827) suggests the sheet comes from the late 1820s or later. No mathematical analysis of the knots, such as crossing codes or invariants, appears on this page.

results.what: Drawings of practical knots: weaver's knot (sheet bend), carrick bend, a loop knot (bowline-type), a hitch, and an ornamental four-lobed knot. There is no accompanying mathematics.
results.modern_name: Knot diagrams of bends, hitches and loops; physical precursors of knot projections in knot theory
results.usually_credited_to: Traditional seamanship and craft knowledge. Mathematical knot theory is usually traced to Gauss (linking integral, 1833; crossing-sequence notation for curves), Listing (1847), and Tait, Kirkman and Little (1870s onward).

results.what: Bibliographic note referring to a Viennese publication by Riedl (1827).

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's knot sketches in his Nachlass, including drawings captioned 'Weber Kn.', are known to historians of knot theory (e.g. Epple's work on the origins of knot theory; Przytycki's historical surveys). The page contains only drawings of standard practical knots without any mathematical analysis, so it adds nothing beyond documenting an already-known interest.
transcription_corrections: The title word in the bottom line appears to read 'Sehnenwinkel' (or similar, e.g. 'Sehnenwinkel/Schnenwinkel') rather than 'Schürzwinkel'. The image shows 'Sehnenwinkel' in a light cursive; reading uncertain.
There are two 'Weber Kn.' captions: one in ink above the top-right knot, and one in faint pencil below the right-middle knot (not near the top as the transcription's sequence might suggest).
The page contains roughly seven knot drawings (ink and pencil), which the transcription does not mention.
The old number '487/1' is struck through, and the folio number '1' is circled.
